planting.note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed to at least 70°F, in deeply worked, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; give vines 6–10 feet of room to sprawl and handle ripe fruit gently, since the thin, tender rind that gives Bradford its sweetness also makes it far more bruise-prone than commercial shipping melons.

directions: Sow in fertile, well-drained, deeply worked soil in full sun once soil has warmed; keep evenly watered through fruit set and ease off watering as melons near ripeness to concentrate sugars. Bradford Watermelon is a South Carolina heirloom dating to the 1840s, developed by the Bradford family of Sumter County and grown continuously within the family for over 170 years before nurseryman Nat Bradford reintroduced it commercially in the 2010s. Large oblong fruits (often 25–40 pounds) have a distinctive soft, thin rind and exceptionally sweet, deep red flesh — historically prized enough that the whole melon, rind included, was cooked down into watermelon rind preserves and syrup. That same soft rind made it too fragile for the rail-shipping trade of the early 20th century, which nearly drove the variety extinct as tougher-rinded shipping melons took over the commercial market; it survived only because the Bradford family kept saving and replanting seed on their own land. A true living-history heirloom for the home garden, where a thin, easily bruised rind is no obstacle, in zone 4–11.

planting.note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed to at least 65°F, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; provide an 8-foot pole or trellis, since this vigorous semi-runner climbs readily and produces best when given full support.

directions: Sow at the base of poles or a trellis in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; pick young for snap beans, at the shelly stage for a creamy fresh bean, or let pods dry fully on the vine for storage beans. Case Knife is an old Southern heirloom pole bean named for its long, flat, slightly curved pods, which resemble the folding blade of a case knife (a traditional pocketknife). The vigorous vines climb readily to 6–8 feet and bear heavily over a long summer season, producing broad, tender pods best picked young for snap use before the beans inside swell; left to mature, the pods yield plump, cream-white beans that shell out easily and cook to a smooth, buttery texture, or can be dried fully for winter storage. Valued in old Southern gardens for its dependable heat tolerance and heavy yield from a small footprint of trellis space, making it a practical choice for Gulf South vegetable gardens where many bush beans falter in midsummer heat.

planting.note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably above 55°F. In zone 9, Creole tomato is also widely grown as a fall crop from a mid-to-late-summer sowing for harvest before the first frost.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and stake or cage for support; consistent moisture prevents blossom end rot and cracking in humid conditions. Creole is an indeterminate tomato developed by the LSU AgCenter specifically for the heat, humidity, and disease pressure of the lower Mississippi River valley, and it gave its name to the famous 'Creole tomatoes' grown in the rich alluvial soil of Louisiana's river parishes and sold at the long-running French Market in New Orleans. It sets fruit reliably even through the hot, muggy stretches of a Gulf South summer that cause many other tomatoes to drop blossoms, and carries useful resistance to fusarium wilt and other soilborne diseases common in southern gardens. The medium-large, deep red, globe-shaped fruits have the rich, well-balanced sweet-acid flavor that built the Creole tomato's regional reputation, celebrated every June at the New Orleans French Market Creole Tomato Festival. A dependable, disease-resistant choice for zone 4–11 gardeners who want a genuinely Deep South tomato.

planting.note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost with bottom heat; transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after the danger of frost has fully passed and soil has warmed.

directions: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; stake taller plants if heavily loaded with fruit. Peter Pepper is a well-known Southern heirloom hot pepper, famous for its unmistakably novelty shape, which has made it a popular curiosity and conversation piece for generations of home gardeners across Texas and Louisiana. The medium-heat fruits (roughly 10,000–25,000 Scoville units, comparable to a strong jalapeño or mild cayenne) ripen from green to red and carry a fruity, tangy flavor good in salsas, pickling, and hot sauce once the novelty value has been enjoyed. Plants are productive and reasonably compact, performing well in containers as well as garden beds, and the fruit's thick walls hold up nicely to stuffing or pickling whole. A fun, genuinely productive heirloom for gardeners who want something distinctive alongside their standard pepper lineup, in zone 4–11.

planting.note: Direct sow or set transplants 10–12 weeks before the first fall frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; in zone 9, Morris Heading can also be sown in late winter for a spring crop, but the fall-sown crop is sweetest since frost converts starches to sugars.

directions: Set transplants or thin direct-sown seedlings to 24–30 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; wider spacing than most collards is needed because Morris Heading forms a loose, cabbage-like head rather than a simple open rosette of leaves. This old Southern heirloom collard is distinctive among collard varieties for its semi-heading habit — the inner leaves cup and fold inward to form a loose head reminiscent of a savoy cabbage, while the outer leaves remain harvestable individually as with any collard. The smooth, tender, blue-green leaves have a sweeter, milder flavor than many open-leaf collard varieties, and the heading habit helps blanch and protect the inner leaves from cold and insect damage. Long grown in home gardens across the Carolinas and Georgia, it is well suited to the mild winters of the Gulf South, where fall-planted crops can be harvested over many months. Zone 6–10.
